question: How many protected classes are recognized under the federal Fair Housing Act as amended?
choice_a: Five — race, color, religion, sex, and national origin
choice_b: Six — race, color, religion, national origin, familial status, and disability
choice_c: Eight — race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, and age
choice_d: Seven — race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability
explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added familial status and disability to the five classes protected under the original 1968 Act, bringing the total to seven federally protected classes.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3604; Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988

question: The federal Fair Housing Act was originally enacted as part of which law?
choice_a: Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968
choice_b: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
choice_c: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974
choice_d: The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977
explanation: The Fair Housing Act is Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, later amended in 1988 to add familial status and disability protections.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3601 et seq.

question: Which federal agency has primary responsibility for enforcing the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
choice_b: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
choice_c: The Department of Justice's Antitrust Division
choice_d: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
explanation: HUD investigates and processes Fair Housing Act complaints; the Department of Justice handles pattern-or-practice cases and cases referred by HUD.

question: "Familial status" as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act primarily protects...
choice_a: Only married couples with biological children
choice_b: Single individuals without children
choice_c: Households with one or more children under age 18, including pregnant women and people securing legal custody of children
choice_d: Households headed by a grandparent
explanation: Familial status protects families with children under 18 in the household, pregnant women, and those in the process of securing legal custody of a minor.

question: Under the Fair Housing Act, "disability" (handicap) is defined to include...
choice_a: Only permanent physical impairments visible to others
choice_b: Only conditions officially certified by a physician as a legal disability
choice_c: Temporary illnesses lasting less than 90 days
choice_d: A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities
explanation: The FHA defines disability broadly to include physical or mental impairments substantially limiting major life activities, a record of such impairment, or being regarded as having such impairment.

question: A landlord refuses to rent to a family because their four children would "make too much noise." This refusal is most likely a violation based on which protected class?
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: National origin
choice_c: Disability
choice_d: Religion
explanation: Refusing to rent to a household because it includes children implicates the familial status protection under the Fair Housing Act.

question: A reasonable accommodation request under the Fair Housing Act for a tenant with a disability would most likely require a landlord to...
choice_a: Reduce the tenant's rent
choice_b: Allow a service or assistance animal despite an otherwise applicable "no pets" policy
choice_c: Guarantee the tenant the parking space closest to the building regardless of demonstrated need
choice_d: Automatically extend the lease term indefinitely
explanation: Waiving a no-pets policy to permit a needed assistance animal is a classic example of a required reasonable accommodation; rent reductions and indefinite lease extensions are not required accommodations.

question: Which of the following is an exemption from the Fair Housing Act's prohibitions, though it does NOT permit discriminatory advertising?
choice_a: Any apartment complex with fewer than 50 units
choice_b: Any single-family home, regardless of who sells it or how it is advertised
choice_c: An owner-occupied dwelling with no more than four units, where the owner lives in one of the units
choice_d: Any rental to a family member, even in a large complex
explanation: The so-called "Mrs. Murphy" exemption applies to owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units where no broker is used, but the ban on discriminatory advertising still applies even under this exemption.

question: The "private club" exemption to the Fair Housing Act allows...
choice_a: Any club or association to refuse to rent to any protected class for any reason
choice_b: Real estate brokers to discriminate whenever representing club members
choice_c: Country clubs to discriminate in their employment decisions
choice_d: A bona fide private club to limit rental or occupancy of lodgings it owns to its own members for other than a commercial purpose
explanation: The private club exemption is narrow: it applies only to noncommercial lodgings a bona fide private club owns and limits to its own members.

question: Religious organizations may limit the sale, rental, or occupancy of dwellings they own to persons of the same religion when...
choice_a: The dwelling is owned or operated for a noncommercial purpose and membership in the religion is not restricted based on race, color, or national origin
choice_b: They obtain a special HUD waiver each calendar year
choice_c: They operate the housing for profit
choice_d: The applicant belongs to any religion at all
explanation: The religious organization exemption requires noncommercial operation and that the religion itself does not restrict membership by race, color, or national origin.

question: Which protected class under the Fair Housing Act has effectively no statutory exemption available, meaning discrimination based on it is never lawful even under exemptions like the owner-occupied or single-family provisions?
choice_a: Religion
choice_b: Race
choice_c: Familial status
choice_d: Disability
explanation: None of the Fair Housing Act's exemptions shield race discrimination, and the Civil Rights Act of 1866 independently bars all racial discrimination in property transactions with no exemptions whatsoever.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §1982; Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)

question: Following the reasoning of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020), which extended Title VII's sex-discrimination protections to sexual orientation and gender identity, HUD has taken the position that housing discrimination on those bases is addressed under which existing Fair Housing Act protected class?
choice_a: National origin
choice_b: Familial status
choice_c: Sex
choice_d: Religion
explanation: HUD's February 2021 memorandum directs that Fair Housing Act complaints alleging discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity be investigated as sex discrimination, applying Bostock's reasoning.
source_note: HUD Memorandum, Feb. 11, 2021; Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644 (2020)

question: A landlord refuses to rent an apartment to an applicant after learning the applicant is transgender. Under current HUD guidance, this refusal is treated as...
choice_a: Conduct not covered by any federal fair housing protection
choice_b: A violation only if the state has its own specific gender identity statute
choice_c: Permissible so long as the landlord cites a general personal objection
choice_d: Sex discrimination prohibited under the Fair Housing Act
explanation: HUD guidance treats discrimination against transgender individuals as sex discrimination prohibited under the Fair Housing Act, regardless of whether state law separately addresses gender identity.
source_note: HUD Memorandum, Feb. 11, 2021

question: HUD's Equal Access Rule requires that HUD-assisted and HUD-insured housing programs be made available without regard to...
choice_a: Actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, or marital status
choice_b: Marital status only
choice_c: Sexual orientation only
choice_d: Household income
explanation: The Equal Access Rule extends equal access in HUD programs to LGBTQ individuals and families regardless of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, or marital status.
source_note: 24 CFR Part 5 (Equal Access Rule, as amended)

question: "Blockbusting" under the Fair Housing Act refers to...
choice_a: Refusing to make loans in a particular neighborhood based on its racial composition
choice_b: Inducing owners to sell or rent by suggesting that persons of a particular protected class are entering the neighborhood, causing property values to decline
choice_c: Directing homebuyers toward or away from certain neighborhoods based on protected class
choice_d: Charging different commission rates to different clients
explanation: Blockbusting is the practice of inducing panic selling by suggesting that the entry of a protected class into a neighborhood will lower property values or increase crime.

question: "Steering" is best described as...
choice_a: A lender refusing to lend in minority neighborhoods
choice_b: An owner refusing to sell to a specific buyer
choice_c: A real estate licensee directing prospective buyers toward or away from particular neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic
choice_d: A broker charging a discounted commission
explanation: Steering occurs when a licensee limits or influences a buyer's or renter's housing choices based on a protected class, whether by encouraging or discouraging interest in particular areas.

question: "Redlining" is a discriminatory practice most closely associated with...
choice_a: Brokers advertising listings only to certain racial groups
choice_b: Sellers refusing to consider multiple competing offers
choice_c: Appraisers inflating property values
choice_d: Lenders or insurers denying or limiting services in specific geographic areas based on the racial or ethnic composition of residents
explanation: Redlining refers to the discriminatory denial or limitation of financial services, such as mortgage lending or insurance, based on the demographic makeup of a geographic area rather than individual creditworthiness.
source_note: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act; Equal Credit Opportunity Act enforcement context

question: "Disparate treatment" discrimination under the Fair Housing Act occurs when...
choice_a: A person is intentionally treated differently because of their membership in a protected class
choice_b: A facially neutral policy has a disproportionate negative effect on a protected class, regardless of intent
choice_c: A landlord applies identical screening criteria to every applicant
choice_d: A broker charges a uniform commission rate to all clients
explanation: Disparate treatment requires intentional differential treatment based on protected class status, which distinguishes it from disparate impact, where a neutral policy has an unjustified discriminatory effect without necessarily requiring discriminatory intent.
source_note: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

question: "Disparate impact" liability under the Fair Housing Act can arise even when...
choice_a: There is direct evidence of intentional discrimination
choice_b: A housing policy is neutral on its face but has an unjustified discriminatory effect on a protected class
choice_c: No protected class is affected by the policy
choice_d: The policy affects only the property owner and no one else
explanation: The Supreme Court confirmed that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, allowing liability for facially neutral policies that cause an unjustified discriminatory effect, without requiring proof of discriminatory intent.
source_note: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

question: A real estate agent tells an African American couple that a listing "just went under contract" while telling a white couple the same day that the identical home is still available. This is an example of...
choice_a: Blockbusting
choice_b: Redlining
choice_c: Disparate treatment through discriminatory misrepresentation of availability
choice_d: A permissible business practice
explanation: Falsely representing that a dwelling is unavailable because of a prospective buyer's protected class status is expressly prohibited disparate treatment under the Fair Housing Act.

question: Which of the following is prohibited under the Fair Housing Act's advertising provisions, regardless of the advertiser's actual intent to discriminate?
choice_a: Advertising the square footage of a home
choice_b: Advertising the sale price of a home
choice_c: Listing the number of bedrooms and bathrooms
choice_d: Publishing a real estate advertisement that indicates a preference or limitation based on a protected class
explanation: Section 3604(c) prohibits advertisements that indicate any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class, and courts apply an objective standard so intent is not required.

question: The Equal Housing Opportunity logo and slogan are used in real estate marketing to...
choice_a: Signal a firm's compliance with and commitment to fair housing laws in its advertising and marketing materials
choice_b: Indicate that a property is government-subsidized housing
choice_c: Certify that a home meets ADA accessibility standards
choice_d: Show that a broker charges a discounted commission
explanation: HUD's Equal Housing Opportunity logo and slogan communicate a firm's commitment to fair housing compliance and are recommended for use in real estate advertising.
source_note: HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines, 24 CFR Part 109

question: Under HUD advertising guidelines, which phrase in a rental listing would most likely violate the Fair Housing Act?
choice_a: "Close to public transportation"
choice_b: "Perfect for a Christian family"
choice_c: "Newly renovated kitchen"
choice_d: "Available immediately"
explanation: Language expressing a religious preference in housing advertising violates Section 3604(c); neutral descriptions of the property or its location generally do not.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3604(c); HUD Fair Housing Advertising Guidelines

question: Real estate advertising describing a neighborhood as "walking distance to the synagogue" and "ideal for young professionals, no kids" raises fair housing concerns because it may express an unlawful preference based on...
choice_a: Price and location only
choice_b: Square footage
choice_c: Religion and familial status
choice_d: Nothing — all location-based descriptions are always permitted
explanation: Language that implies a preference for or against a religious group, or that discourages households with children, can violate the Fair Housing Act's advertising prohibitions.

question: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) primarily requires real estate brokerage offices, as places of public accommodation, to...
choice_a: Retrofit every residential rental unit they manage for full wheelchair accessibility
choice_b: Provide free housing to disabled tenants
choice_c: Waive application fees for disabled applicants
choice_d: Remove architectural barriers where readily achievable so members of the public can access the office
explanation: ADA Title III governs commercial facilities and places of public accommodation, such as brokerage offices, requiring barrier removal where readily achievable; it does not itself mandate residential unit retrofits.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §12181 et seq. (ADA Title III)

question: Which federal law imposes accessible design and construction requirements on new multifamily housing with four or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991?
choice_a: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 design and construction requirements
choice_b: The Americans with Disabilities Act
choice_c: The Rehabilitation Act of 1973
choice_d: The Uniform Federal Accessibility Standards Act
explanation: The 1988 Fair Housing Amendments Act, not the ADA, imposes accessible design and construction standards on covered new multifamily dwellings with four or more units.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3604(f)(3)(C); Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988

question: A real estate brokerage's public-facing website would most likely need to consider accessibility obligations, such as screen-reader compatibility, under...
choice_a: The Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements only
choice_b: ADA Title III, as courts and DOJ guidance increasingly treat websites of places of public accommodation as covered
choice_c: The Sherman Antitrust Act
choice_d: No federal law addresses website accessibility
explanation: DOJ guidance and a growing body of case law treat websites operated by places of public accommodation, including real estate brokerages, as potentially subject to ADA Title III accessibility obligations.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §12182 (ADA Title III); DOJ website accessibility guidance

question: For federal tax purposes, a real estate licensee generally qualifies as an independent contractor rather than an employee when, among other conditions, substantially all of the licensee's pay is based on...
choice_a: Seniority within the firm
choice_b: A fixed annual salary
choice_c: Sales output or production rather than hours worked
choice_d: Hours worked, similar to an hourly employee
explanation: The federal statutory safe harbor for qualified real estate agents requires that substantially all compensation be tied to sales or output rather than hours worked, among other conditions.
source_note: 26 U.S.C. §3508 (qualified real estate agent safe harbor)

question: Under the federal statutory safe harbor for qualified real estate agents, a written contract between a broker and a licensee must state that the licensee...
choice_a: Is guaranteed a minimum hourly wage
choice_b: Is entitled to employee fringe benefits
choice_c: Must work fixed office hours set by the broker
choice_d: Will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes
explanation: One of the three required elements of the federal safe harbor is a written contract providing that the licensee will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes.

question: Which classification issue determines whether a broker must withhold payroll taxes and provide workers' compensation coverage for a licensee?
choice_a: Whether the licensee is properly classified as an employee versus an independent contractor
choice_b: Whether the licensee sells residential or commercial property
choice_c: Whether the licensee has held a license for more than five years
choice_d: The licensee's total annual sales volume
explanation: Employee-versus-independent-contractor classification, not property type, tenure, or sales volume, determines payroll tax withholding and workers' compensation obligations.
source_note: 26 U.S.C. §3508; general federal/state employment classification principles

question: Real estate brokers who agree among themselves to charge a uniform commission rate would most likely violate the Sherman Antitrust Act under the theory of...
choice_a: Group boycott
choice_b: Price fixing
choice_c: Tie-in arrangement
choice_d: Market allocation
explanation: Horizontal agreements among competing brokers to set or standardize commission rates constitute per se illegal price fixing under Section 1 of the Sherman Act.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1 (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1)

question: Two competing brokerages agree that one will only take listings on the north side of town while the other operates only on the south side. This agreement is an antitrust violation known as...
choice_a: Price fixing
choice_b: Tying arrangement
choice_c: Market allocation
choice_d: Steering
explanation: Agreements between competitors to divide territories or customers constitute illegal market allocation under the Sherman Act.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1 (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1)

question: A group of brokers agrees to refuse to show homes listed by a discount brokerage or to exclude it from cooperative arrangements. This coordinated refusal is an antitrust violation known as...
choice_a: Price fixing
choice_b: Market allocation
choice_c: Redlining
choice_d: Group boycott
explanation: A coordinated agreement among competitors to exclude or refuse to deal with another firm is a group boycott, a form of unlawful concerted action under the Sherman Act.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1 (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1)

question: Requiring a home buyer to use a seller-affiliated title company as a condition of purchasing the home may raise antitrust concerns under the theory of...
choice_a: An illegal tying arrangement
choice_b: Blockbusting
choice_c: Steering
choice_d: Redlining
explanation: Conditioning the purchase of one product or service (the home) on the purchase of another (a specific title company's services) can constitute an illegal tying arrangement under antitrust law.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1 (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1)

question: Under the Sherman Antitrust Act, criminal penalties for a corporate violation can include fines up to...
choice_a: $10,000 with no possibility of imprisonment
choice_b: $100 million for corporations, with individuals facing fines up to $1 million and up to 10 years imprisonment
choice_c: A civil fine only, capped at $5,000
choice_d: License revocation only, with no monetary penalty
explanation: The Sherman Act, as amended, authorizes substantial criminal penalties: up to $100 million for corporations and up to $1 million plus up to 10 years imprisonment for individuals, in addition to potential treble damages in civil suits.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1, as amended by the Antitrust Criminal Penalty Enhancement and Reform Act of 2004

question: The National Do Not Call Registry is established and enforced primarily under...
choice_a: The Fair Housing Act
choice_b: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
choice_c: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act and the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule
choice_d: The Sherman Antitrust Act
explanation: The National Do Not Call Registry operates under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, enforced by the FTC and FCC.
source_note: 47 U.S.C. §227 (TCPA); 16 CFR Part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule)

question: A real estate licensee may still call a consumer whose number is on the National Do Not Call Registry if...
choice_a: The licensee simply believes the consumer might be interested in buying
choice_b: The call is placed after 9:00 p.m. local time
choice_c: The licensee has never spoken with the consumer before
choice_d: The consumer has an established business relationship with the licensee within the preceding 18 months
explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule provides an established business relationship exemption allowing calls to consumers with whom the caller has transacted business within the prior 18 months, even if the number is registered.

question: If a consumer submits a written request to a specific real estate firm asking not to be called again, that firm must honor the request for...
choice_a: A minimum of five years, or permanently if the firm's own policy so provides
choice_b: 30 days only
choice_c: The remainder of the current calendar year only
choice_d: There is no specific legally required period
explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule requires a company-specific do-not-call request to be honored for at least five years, and many firms adopt a permanent internal policy.

question: When a real estate licensee posts a paid or sponsored ad on social media for a listing, best compliance practice under advertising regulations requires the licensee to...
choice_a: Avoid disclosing their license status to appear more approachable
choice_b: Clearly disclose their name and firm, consistent with state advertising rules applicable to any other form of advertisement
choice_c: Use only a personal social media account, never a business page
choice_d: Omit the brokerage name to keep posts concise
explanation: Social media and internet advertising are generally held to the same license-law advertising disclosure standards as traditional print or broadcast media, including identifying the licensee and firm.
source_note: General state license-law advertising disclosure requirements applicable to internet/social media advertising

question: A licensee's social media posts and blog content promoting listings are generally considered "advertising" and are therefore subject to...
choice_a: No regulation at all, since social media is a personal platform
choice_b: Only federal securities law
choice_c: The same truth-in-advertising and fair housing compliance standards as traditional print or broadcast advertising
choice_d: Only the social media platform's own terms of service
explanation: Regulators treat internet and social media marketing of real estate as advertising subject to the same fair housing and truth-in-advertising standards that apply to any other medium.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3604(c); state advertising regulations

question: Unsolicited commercial email sent by a licensee to promote listings must comply with which federal law governing commercial email?
choice_a: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act
choice_b: The Fair Credit Reporting Act
choice_c: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
choice_d: The CAN-SPAM Act
explanation: The CAN-SPAM Act sets requirements for commercial email, including accurate header information, a clear opt-out mechanism, and honoring opt-out requests promptly.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §7701 et seq. (CAN-SPAM Act)

question: A licensee's duty to protect a client's confidential personal information, such as financial condition or motivation to sell, generally...
choice_a: Continues even after the agency relationship or transaction has ended, unless disclosure is required by law or authorized by the client
choice_b: Ends automatically the moment the transaction closes
choice_c: Applies only to information received in writing, not information learned verbally
choice_d: Applies only to seller clients, never to buyer clients
explanation: Fiduciary confidentiality duties generally survive the termination of the agency relationship, continuing to protect a client's confidential information unless disclosure is legally required or the client consents.
source_note: General fiduciary duty principles applicable to real estate agency relationships

question: Which of the following would be an appropriate exception permitting a licensee to disclose a client's confidential information without breaching fiduciary duty?
choice_a: Disclosing the information to a friend socially, in confidence
choice_b: Disclosure required by law, such as in response to a valid subpoena, or made with the client's informed consent
choice_c: Posting the client's financial details on the brokerage's public website for marketing purposes
choice_d: Sharing the information with a competing brokerage to build goodwill
explanation: Legally compelled disclosure or the client's own informed consent are recognized exceptions to a licensee's duty of confidentiality; voluntary disclosure to third parties for the licensee's own convenience is not.
source_note: General fiduciary duty principles applicable to real estate agency relationships

question: A broker who receives earnest money from a buyer must generally...
choice_a: Deposit the funds into the broker's personal checking account for safekeeping
choice_b: Hold the cash in the office safe indefinitely with no accounting requirement
choice_c: Deposit the funds into a separate trust or escrow account and never commingle them with personal or brokerage operating funds
choice_d: Immediately disburse the funds to the seller before closing
explanation: Trust or escrow accounting rules universally require brokers to hold clients' and customers' funds in a separate account and prohibit commingling those funds with the broker's own operating funds.
source_note: General trust/escrow account requirements common to real estate license law

question: Using client trust or escrow funds for the broker's own business expenses, even temporarily and with intent to repay, is known as...
choice_a: Steering
choice_b: A permissible short-term bridge loan practice
choice_c: Disparate treatment
choice_d: Conversion, a serious licensing violation that can also constitute a crime
explanation: Using client trust funds for any purpose other than the client's benefit is conversion, a serious violation that can result in license revocation and criminal prosecution, regardless of intent to repay.
source_note: General trust/escrow account requirements common to real estate license law

question: A broker's duty regarding funds belonging to others generally includes...
choice_a: Maintaining accurate records and providing timely accounting and reconciliation of trust account transactions
choice_b: Investing trust funds in the stock market to earn interest for the brokerage
choice_c: Mixing multiple clients' escrow deposits into a single account with no individual recordkeeping
choice_d: Maintaining records only if a client specifically requests them
explanation: Trust account rules require brokers to keep accurate, itemized records for each client's funds and to reconcile the account regularly, regardless of whether a client requests an accounting.
source_note: General trust/escrow account requirements common to real estate license law

question: A licensee's duty of due diligence in a transaction generally requires the licensee to...
choice_a: Conduct an engineering-level structural inspection of every property personally
choice_b: Visually inspect reasonably accessible areas of the property and disclose known or reasonably discoverable material facts
choice_c: Rely exclusively on the seller's representations without any independent inquiry
choice_d: Have no obligation regarding property condition, since that is solely the home inspector's job
explanation: Due diligence requires a reasonable visual inspection of accessible areas and disclosure of known or reasonably discoverable material facts, falling short of an expert-level inspection but exceeding blind reliance on the seller.
source_note: General due diligence and disclosure duty principles applicable to real estate licensees

question: If a licensee becomes aware of information suggesting a material defect that contradicts the seller's disclosure statement, the licensee's due diligence duty requires the licensee to...
choice_a: Disregard the information because the seller's written disclosure controls regardless of contrary facts
choice_b: Disclose it only if the buyer specifically asks about that exact defect
choice_c: Investigate further and ensure the discrepancy is disclosed to the buyer, rather than ignoring it
choice_d: Report it only to the seller, with no corresponding duty toward the buyer
explanation: A licensee who becomes aware of facts contradicting a seller's disclosure cannot simply rely on the seller's statement and must investigate and ensure the buyer receives accurate, material information.
source_note: General due diligence and disclosure duty principles applicable to real estate licensees

question: A designated broker's supervisory responsibility over affiliated licensees generally includes...
choice_a: No responsibility once a licensee is affiliated, since each licensee is independently liable for their own conduct
choice_b: Personally attending every showing and closing conducted by affiliated licensees
choice_c: Supervising only those licensees classified as employees, not independent contractors
choice_d: Reviewing transaction documents, ensuring compliance with license law, and providing reasonable oversight and training
explanation: Brokers remain responsible for reasonable supervision of all affiliated licensees, including reviewing transaction paperwork and ensuring compliance with license law, regardless of whether a licensee is classified as an employee or an independent contractor for tax purposes.
source_note: General broker supervisory responsibility principles under real estate license law

question: An unlicensed personal assistant working for a broker may generally perform which of the following tasks without violating license law?
choice_a: Scheduling appointments and distributing pre-printed marketing flyers
choice_b: Negotiating contract terms with a prospective buyer
choice_c: Hosting an open house and answering questions about price or terms
choice_d: Discussing commission rates with a client
explanation: Unlicensed assistants may perform purely clerical and administrative tasks, such as scheduling and distributing pre-approved flyers, but may not negotiate, discuss price or terms, or otherwise perform activities that require a real estate license, and the supervising broker is responsible for enforcing this boundary.
source_note: General unlicensed assistant activity limits under real estate license law

question: A broker who fails to adequately supervise licensees affiliated with the firm, resulting in license law violations by those licensees, may...
choice_a: Never be held responsible, since only the individual licensee who committed the violation can be disciplined
choice_b: Face disciplinary action against the broker's own license, in addition to any action taken against the individual licensee
choice_c: Only face a civil lawsuit, never license discipline
choice_d: Only be held responsible if the broker personally directed the specific violation
explanation: Because brokers are responsible for supervising affiliated licensees, inadequate supervision that permits violations can expose the broker's own license to discipline independent of any action against the individual licensee.
source_note: General broker supervisory responsibility principles under real estate license law

question: Before the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added familial status and disability, which protected class had been added to the Fair Housing Act by a 1974 amendment?
choice_a: National origin
choice_b: Age
choice_c: Sex
choice_d: Marital status
explanation: The original 1968 Act covered race, color, religion, and national origin. The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex as a protected class, well before familial status and disability were added in 1988.
source_note: Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, Pub. L. 93-383; 42 U.S.C. §3604

question: The Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) exemption from the Fair Housing Act's familial-status protections applies to...
choice_a: All rental housing where the majority of tenants happen to be over 55
choice_b: Any housing community that markets itself as "adult living," regardless of actual occupancy
choice_c: An exemption from all seven federally protected classes for residents over 62
choice_d: Qualifying senior housing communities, exempting them only from familial-status discrimination claims, not from any other protected class
explanation: HOPA's exemption is narrow: it exempts only qualifying 55-and-older or 62-and-older housing from familial-status claims. Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, and disability protections remain fully applicable.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3607(b); Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995

question: To qualify as "55 and older" housing under HOPA's familial-status exemption, a community must, among other requirements...
choice_a: Have at least 80% of its occupied units with at least one resident age 55 or older
choice_b: House residents who are all at least 55 with absolutely no exceptions
choice_c: Have at least 50% of occupied units with a resident 55 or older
choice_d: Simply advertise itself as a 55+ community, with no occupancy verification required
explanation: HOPA's 55-and-older exemption requires at least 80% of occupied units to have one occupant 55 or older, published policies demonstrating intent to operate as 55+ housing, and compliance with HUD's age-verification procedures.

question: The key distinction between a "reasonable accommodation" and a "reasonable modification" under the Fair Housing Act is that...
choice_a: An accommodation always requires the landlord to pay, while a modification is always free to the landlord
choice_b: An accommodation is a change to rules, policies, or services, while a modification is a structural or physical change to the premises
choice_c: There is no legal distinction between the two terms
choice_d: A modification applies only to commercial property, never to residential property
explanation: Accommodations involve changing rules or policies (such as waiving a no-pets policy); modifications are physical or structural changes to a dwelling or common area (such as installing a ramp). In private, non-federally-funded housing the tenant generally bears the cost of a reasonable modification, unlike a reasonable accommodation.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §3604(f)(3)(A)-(B); Joint HUD/DOJ Statements on Reasonable Accommodations (2004) and Reasonable Modifications (2008)

question: Under HUD's assistance animal guidance, the category of animals that must be reasonably accommodated in housing under the Fair Housing Act is...
choice_a: Identical to the ADA's definition, limited to dogs individually trained to perform specific tasks
choice_b: Limited strictly to animals certified by a state licensing board
choice_c: Broader than the ADA's definition of "service animal," and may include emotional support animals that provide a disability-related benefit even without individualized task training
choice_d: Limited to animals meeting a specific weight or breed restriction set by HUD
explanation: HUD's 2020 Assistance Animal Notice confirms that assistance animals protected under the FHA include emotional support animals, not just trained service animals, making the FHA category broader than the ADA's narrower service-animal definition.
source_note: HUD Notice FHEO-2020-01 (Assessing a Person's Request to Have an Animal as a Reasonable Accommodation)

question: A housing provider may lawfully deny a requested reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act when...
choice_a: The provider simply prefers not to deal with tenants who have disabilities
choice_b: The accommodation would be somewhat inconvenient for staff
choice_c: The tenant's disability is one the provider considers embarrassing to other residents
choice_d: The individual poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others that cannot be eliminated or reduced by another reasonable accommodation
explanation: The FHA's direct-threat exception is narrow and requires an individualized assessment showing a genuine, unmitigable threat to health or safety; general discomfort or inconvenience does not qualify.

question: HUD's Quid Pro Quo and Hostile Environment Harassment rule provides that...
choice_a: Both quid pro quo harassment and unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to create a hostile housing environment constitute unlawful sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act
choice_b: Only physical contact can constitute prohibited harassment under the Fair Housing Act
choice_c: Harassment claims fall outside HUD's jurisdiction and may only be pursued in state court
choice_d: A single isolated joke of a sexual nature always creates Fair Housing Act liability regardless of severity
explanation: HUD's harassment rule codifies that conditioning housing benefits on submission to unwelcome conduct (quid pro quo) and conduct severe or pervasive enough to create a hostile housing environment are both actionable as sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.

question: HUD's Advertising Guidelines for Equal Housing Opportunity advise that print and broadcast advertisements using human models should...
choice_a: Never include any human models under any circumstances
choice_b: Depict models representative of majority and minority groups in the metropolitan area, rather than exclusively one race or group
choice_c: Feature only models who are current tenants of the advertised property
choice_d: Feature models exclusively from the market's majority racial group to appeal to the broadest audience
explanation: HUD's advertising guidelines recommend that models used in real estate advertising reflect the diversity of majority and minority groups in the relevant market so the ad does not suggest a discriminatory preference.
source_note: 24 CFR Part 109, Appendix I (Advertising Guidelines for Equal Housing Opportunity)

question: A person alleging a Fair Housing Act violation generally must file an administrative complaint with HUD within...
choice_a: 30 days of the alleged discriminatory housing practice, with no option to sue in court afterward
choice_b: Ten years of the alleged discriminatory housing practice
choice_c: One year of the alleged discriminatory housing practice, or instead file a civil action in court within two years
choice_d: There is no deadline for filing a Fair Housing Act complaint
explanation: The Fair Housing Act sets a one-year deadline for filing a HUD administrative complaint and a separate two-year statute of limitations for a private civil action in federal or state court.

question: After HUD issues a charge of discrimination following a fair housing complaint, a party to the case may elect to have the matter decided instead by...
choice_a: A binding private arbitrator chosen by HUD
choice_b: The state real estate commission exclusively
choice_c: The complainant's local city council
choice_d: A federal district court judge, rather than a HUD administrative law judge
explanation: After HUD issues a charge, either party may elect within the statutory period to have the case heard in federal district court instead of before a HUD administrative law judge, at which point the Department of Justice may pursue the case on the complainant's behalf.

question: When the Department of Justice brings a "pattern or practice" lawsuit under the Fair Housing Act, the available remedies can include...
choice_a: Injunctive relief, monetary damages for aggrieved persons, and civil penalties to vindicate the public interest
choice_b: Only a formal warning letter, with no other consequence
choice_c: Criminal imprisonment of the individual licensee only, with no other remedy available
choice_d: Direct revocation of the defendant's real estate license by the Department of Justice
explanation: DOJ pattern-or-practice suits under Section 3614 can yield injunctive relief, damages for aggrieved persons, and civil penalties; DOJ does not itself revoke real estate licenses, which remains a state licensing function.

question: Under the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992, sellers and landlords of "target housing" built before 1978 must...
choice_a: Remove all lead-based paint from the property before any sale or lease can occur
choice_b: Disclose known lead-based paint hazards, provide any available records, distribute an EPA-approved pamphlet, and give buyers a 10-day opportunity to test for lead before becoming obligated under a purchase contract
choice_c: Obtain a state lead-abatement permit before advertising the property
choice_d: Disclose lead-paint hazards only if the buyer specifically requests such information in writing
explanation: Title X requires disclosure of known lead-based paint information, distribution of an EPA pamphlet, and, for sales, a 10-day inspection opportunity for target housing built before 1978, but it does not require abatement or removal as a precondition of sale or lease.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §4852d; Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992; 24 CFR Part 35, 40 CFR Part 745

question: Following the 2024 nationwide settlement of commission-related antitrust litigation involving the National Association of REALTORS, MLS participants working with buyers are now generally required to...
choice_a: Charge every buyer client an identical, association-mandated commission rate
choice_b: Refuse to work with any buyer who declines to sign an exclusive agreement
choice_c: Enter into a written buyer representation agreement specifying compensation before touring homes with the buyer, and offers of buyer-broker compensation may no longer be published on the MLS
choice_d: Publish every agent's commission rate on a federal government website
explanation: The 2024 settlement arising from the Sitzer/Burnett-related litigation requires MLS participants to have a signed written buyer agreement before touring homes and removed the practice of publishing buyer-broker compensation offers on the MLS, while leaving commission rates fully negotiable rather than fixed.
source_note: NAR nationwide settlement agreement, effective August 17, 2024

question: Several competing brokerages in a market independently, without any agreement or communication among them, all charge similar commission rates because that rate is typical for the market. Standing alone, this "conscious parallelism" is...
choice_a: Automatically illegal price fixing, regardless of whether any agreement existed
choice_b: Illegal only if fewer than three brokerages are involved
choice_c: Illegal exclusively under the Fair Housing Act rather than antitrust law
choice_d: Not automatically a Sherman Act violation, because unlawful price fixing requires proof of an actual agreement or concerted action, not merely similar independent conduct
explanation: Antitrust liability for price fixing requires proof of an agreement or concerted action among competitors; independently charging similar rates without collusion does not, by itself, establish a Sherman Act violation.
source_note: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007); 15 U.S.C. §1

question: Which of the following commission-related practices does NOT, by itself, violate federal antitrust law?
choice_a: An individual broker unilaterally deciding, without any agreement with a competitor, what commission rate to charge its own clients
choice_b: Two competing brokers agreeing in advance on the commission rate both will charge
choice_c: A group of brokers agreeing to boycott any client who negotiates a lower commission
choice_d: A trade association publishing a mandatory commission schedule its members are told to follow
explanation: Antitrust law does not restrict what an individual firm charges when set unilaterally; the Sherman Act targets agreements or concerted action among competitors, such as horizontal price fixing, boycotts, or association-mandated fee schedules.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §1 (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1)

question: When a third party posts a discriminatory rental advertisement on an online listing platform, courts applying Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act have generally held that...
choice_a: The platform is always strictly liable for any discriminatory content posted by any user
choice_b: The platform hosting the user-generated content is typically shielded from Fair Housing Act liability, while the individual who authored the discriminatory ad remains liable
choice_c: Section 230 eliminates Fair Housing Act liability for everyone involved, including the ad's author
choice_d: Section 230 applies only to print newspapers, not websites
explanation: Courts, including the Seventh Circuit in the Craigslist litigation, have held that Section 230 generally immunizes interactive online platforms from liability for discriminatory content authored by third-party users, while the author of the ad remains liable under the Fair Housing Act.
source_note: 47 U.S.C. §230; Chicago Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law v. Craigslist, Inc., 519 F.3d 666 (7th Cir. 2008)

question: Under the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, a real estate licensee making outbound sales calls to a consumer may generally only call between...
choice_a: 6:00 a.m. and 11:00 p.m. local time, with no further restriction
choice_b: Any hour, as long as the call is answered
choice_c: 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time at the called party's location
choice_d: 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. on weekdays only, with no weekend calls permitted at any hour
explanation: The Telemarketing Sales Rule restricts outbound telemarketing calls to between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time of the called person, regardless of the day of the week.

question: Since a 2008 amendment to federal law, a consumer's phone number placed on the National Do Not Call Registry...
choice_a: Must be re-registered every 90 days to remain active
choice_b: Automatically expires after one year
choice_c: Only protects landline numbers, never cell phones
choice_d: Remains on the registry permanently unless the number is disconnected or the consumer removes it, with no need for periodic re-registration
explanation: The Do-Not-Call Registry Improvement Act of 2007 eliminated the prior five-year re-registration requirement, making registration permanent absent disconnection or voluntary removal; the registry covers both landline and wireless numbers.
source_note: Do-Not-Call Registry Improvement Act of 2007, Pub. L. 110-187

question: A real estate brokerage that is significantly engaged in arranging or providing financial services, such as certain affiliated business arrangements handling consumers' nonpublic personal financial information, may be subject to privacy and data-security obligations under...
choice_a: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's Privacy Rule and Safeguards Rule
choice_b: The Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements
choice_c: The Sherman Antitrust Act
choice_d: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act
explanation: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act imposes privacy-notice and information-safeguarding requirements on "financial institutions," a term FTC rules extend to certain real estate settlement service providers that handle consumers' nonpublic personal financial information.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. §6801 et seq. (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act); 16 CFR Part 314 (Safeguards Rule)

question: If a broker's pooled client trust account earns interest, the broker generally...
choice_a: Automatically owns all interest earned as compensation for handling the funds
choice_b: May not retain that interest for personal or brokerage benefit without proper disclosure and any required client consent or applicable program participation
choice_c: Must immediately close the trust account if it earns any interest at all
choice_d: May deposit the interest into the broker's personal account so long as it is later reported as taxable income
explanation: Because trust funds belong to clients and customers rather than the broker, a broker generally cannot personally profit from interest earned on pooled trust funds without proper disclosure, consent, or participation in a recognized program; doing so otherwise raises the same conversion concerns as misusing principal.
source_note: General trust/escrow account requirements common to real estate license law

question: Whether a real estate licensee is classified as an employee or an independent contractor for federal tax purposes...
choice_a: Determines whether the licensee owes any fiduciary duty at all, with independent contractors owing none
choice_b: Allows an independent contractor licensee to disregard the broker's supervisory authority entirely
choice_c: Has no effect on the fiduciary and license-law duties the licensee owes to clients, customers, and the public
choice_d: Exempts independent contractor licensees from Fair Housing Act compliance
explanation: Tax classification governs matters such as withholding and benefits eligibility; it does not diminish a licensee's fiduciary duties to clients or the broker's supervisory authority and responsibility for compliance with license law and fair housing requirements.
source_note: General principles distinguishing federal tax classification from state license-law fiduciary duties

question: A broker's supervisory responsibility over affiliated licensees generally extends to...
choice_a: Only reviewing advertising placed in printed newspapers, not online or social media content
choice_b: No obligation regarding advertising, since each individual licensee is solely responsible for their own marketing
choice_c: Reviewing advertising only after a consumer complaint has already been filed
choice_d: Reviewing and approving licensee-generated advertising, including social media and internet marketing, for compliance with fair housing and license-law advertising rules
explanation: Because advertising, including social media content, is subject to the same fair housing and license-law standards regardless of medium, a broker's supervisory duty includes reasonable oversight of licensees' marketing to catch and correct compliance problems before they occur.
source_note: General broker supervisory responsibility principles under real estate license law; 42 U.S.C. §3604(c)

question: A licensee's duty of due diligence regarding property condition means the licensee...
choice_a: Is not a guarantor of the property's condition and should recommend that the client obtain a professional inspection for matters beyond the licensee's expertise
choice_b: Personally certifies the structural, mechanical, and electrical soundness of every listed property
choice_c: Has no duty at all once a listing agreement is signed
choice_d: May ignore visible defects in accessible areas because the seller signed a disclosure form
explanation: Due diligence requires reasonable observation and disclosure of readily observable and known material facts, but it does not make the licensee an expert guarantor of condition; recommending qualified professional inspections is the appropriate way to address matters outside a licensee's expertise.
source_note: General due diligence and disclosure duty principles applicable to real estate licensees

question: In addition to removing architectural barriers where readily achievable, Title III of the ADA requires places of public accommodation such as brokerage offices to...
choice_a: Hire a minimum quota of employees with disabilities
choice_b: Provide auxiliary aids and services, such as accessible communication formats, when necessary to ensure effective communication with individuals with disabilities, unless doing so would cause an undue burden or fundamental alteration
choice_c: Provide free housing to any client with a disability
choice_d: Waive standard listing commissions for clients with disabilities
explanation: Title III's effective-communication requirement obligates places of public accommodation to furnish auxiliary aids and services, such as accessible formats or interpreters, when needed, subject to undue-burden and fundamental-alteration limits — a distinct obligation from the physical barrier-removal requirement.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. §12182(b)(2)(A)(iii); 28 CFR §36.303 (ADA Title III effective communication)
